etymologies.etymologyHTML:
From Middle English bush, from Old English busċ, *bysċ (“copse, grove, scrub”, in placenames), from Proto-West Germanic *busk, from Proto-Germanic *buskaz (“bush, thicket”), probably from Proto-Indo-European *bʰuH- (“to grow”). Doublet of bosque.

Cognate with West Frisian bosk (“forest”), Dutch bos (“forest”), German Busch (“bush”), Danish and Norwegian busk (“bush, shrub”), Swedish buske (“bush, shrub”), Persian بیشه (bêša/biše, “woods”). Latin and Romance forms (Latin boscus, Occitan bòsc, French bois, bûche and buisson, Italian bosco and boscaglia, Spanish bosque, Portuguese bosque) derive from the Germanic.

definitions.definition: (horticulture) A woody plant distinguished from a tree by its multiple stems and lower height, being usually less than six metres tall; a horticultural rather than strictly botanical category.

quote.citation: 1913, Joseph C[rosby] Lincoln, chapter I, in Mr. Pratt’s Patients, New York, N.Y., London: D[aniel] Appleton and Company, →OCLC, page 18:
quote.text: I stumbled along through the young pines and huckleberry bushes. Pretty soon I struck into a sort of path that, I cal'lated, might lead to the road I was hunting for. It twisted and turned, and, the first thing I knew, made a sudden bend around a bunch of bayberry scrub and opened out into a big clear space like a lawn.

definitions.definition: A shrub cut off, or a shrublike branch of a tree.
(historical) A shrub or branch, properly, a branch of ivy (sacred to Bacchus), hung out at vintners' doors, or as a tavern sign; hence, a tavern sign, and symbolically, the tavern itself.

quote.citation: c. 1598–1600 (date written), William Shakespeare, “As You Like It”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act V, scene iv], page 207, column 2:
quote.text: If it be true, that good wine needs no buſh, 'tis true, that a good play needes no Epilogue.

quote.citation: 1837, L[etitia] E[lizabeth] L[andon], “Chapter IV. The Fête.”, in Ethel Churchill: Or, The Two Brides. […], volume II, London: Henry Colburn, […], →OCLC, page 31:
quote.text: "Well," replied Lady Mary, "who is to know where good wine is sold, unless you hang out the bush."

definitions.definition: (slang, vulgar) A person's pubic hair, especially a woman's. [from 1745][1]

quote.citation: 1749, [John Cleland], “[Letter the First]”, in Memoirs of a Woman of Pleasure [Fanny Hill], volume I, London:  […]  [Thomas Parker] for G. Fenton [i.e., Fenton and Ralph Griffiths] […], →OCLC, page 65:
quote.text: As he ſtood on one ſide for a minute or ſo, unbuttoning his waſte-coat, and breeches, her fat brawny thighs hung down, and the whole greaſy landſkip lay fairly open to my view: a wide open-mouth’d gap, overſhaded with a grizzly buſh, ſeemed held out like a beggar’s wallet for its’ proviſion.

quote.citation: 1941, Henry Miller, Under the Roofs of Paris (Opus Pistorum), New York: Grove Press, published 1983, page 27:
quote.text: I rub her bush with my cheek and my chin, tickle her bonne-bouche with my tongue.

quote.citation: 1982, Lawrence Durrell, Constance (Avignon Quintet), Faber & Faber, published 2004, page 787:
quote.text: But no, the little pool of semen was there, proof positive, with droplets caught hanging in her bush.

quote.citation: 2002, “The Seed (2.0)”, in Phrenology, performed by The Roots:
quote.text: I push my seed in her bush for life / It's gonna work because I'm pushing it right

definitions.definition: (hunting) The tail, or brush, of a fox.
(intransitive) To branch thickly in the manner of a bush.

quote.citation: 1726, Homer, “The Odyssey”, in Alexander Pope, transl., edited by Samuel Johnson, The Poetical Works of Alexander Pope, Esq., published 1839, page 404:
quote.text: Around it, and above, for ever green, / The bushing alders form'd a shady scene.

definitions.definition: To set bushes for; to support with bushes.
To use a bush harrow on (land), for covering seeds sown; to harrow with a bush.
To become bushy (often used with up).

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From the sign of a bush usually employed to indicate such places.

definitions.definition: (archaic) A tavern or wine merchant.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From older Dutch bosch (modern bos (“wood, forest”)), first appearing in the Dutch colonies to designate an uncleared district of a colony, and thence adopted in British colonies as bush. Could alternatively be interpreted as a semantic loan, as bush (etymology 1) is cognate to the aforementioned archaic Dutch bosch.

definitions.definition: (Australia) The countryside area of Australia that is less arid and less remote than the outback; loosely, areas of natural flora even within conurbations.

quote.citation: 1894, Henry Lawson, “We Called Him “Ally” for Short”, in Short Stories in Prose and Verse‎[1]:
quote.text: I remember, about five years ago, I was greatly annoyed by a ghost, while doing a job of fencing in the bush between here and Perth.

quote.citation: 1899, Ethel C. Pedley, Dot and the Kangaroo‎[2]:
quote.text: Little Dot had lost her way in the bush.

quote.citation: 2000, Robert Holden, Paul Cliff, Jack Bedson, The Endless Playground: Celebrating Australian Childhood, page 16:
quote.text: The theme of children lost in the bush is a well-worked one in Australian art and literature.

quote.citation: 2021 September 6, “Australian farmers under pressure from climate change”, in Australian Herald‎[3]:
quote.text: The findings of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change suggest Australia may have to jettison tracts of the bush unless there is a massive investment in climate-change adaptation and planning.

definitions.definition: (New Zealand) An area of New Zealand covered in forest, especially native forest.
(Canada) The wild forested areas of Canada; upcountry.
(often with "the") Tracts of land covered in natural vegetation that are largely undeveloped and uncultivated.

quote.citation: 1899 February, Joseph Conrad, “The Heart of Darkness”, in Blackwood’s Edinburgh Magazine, volume CLXV, number M, New York, N.Y.: The Leonard Scott Publishing Company, […], →OCLC, part I, page 199:
quote.text: Mad terror had scattered them, men, women, and children, through the bush, and they had never returned.

definitions.definition: (Canada) A wood lot or bluff on a farm.
(Australia) Towards the direction of the outback.
(colloquial) Not skilled; not professional; not major league.
(baseball) Amateurish behavior, short for "bush league behavior"

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle Dutch busse (“box; wheel bushing”), from Proto-West Germanic *buhsā. More at box.

definitions.definition: A thick washer or hollow cylinder of metal.
A mechanical attachment, usually a metallic socket with a screw thread, such as the mechanism by which a camera is attached to a tripod stand.
A piece of copper, screwed into a gun, through which the venthole is bored.
(transitive) To furnish with a bush or lining; to line.
